overview:
The span begins in 802, when a ruler known to later inscriptions as Jayavarman II was consecrated on the Kulen plateau as a universal monarch, an act that Khmer tradition treated as the founding of the kingdom centred on Angkor. Over the next four centuries the plain north of the Tonle Sap filled with royal cities, reservoirs and state temples, an urban and agricultural sprawl of roughly a thousand square kilometres that supported a population usually estimated in the high hundreds of thousands — by area, the largest pre-industrial city known. Its engine was water: enormous rectangular barays and a network of canals and embankments that stored and moved the monsoon, buffering the harvest against bad years. Angkor Wat itself came late in that sequence, begun under Suryavarman II in the first half of the twelfth century as his state temple and probably his funerary monument. Unusually for Angkor, it was dedicated to Vishnu rather than Shiva, and unusually again it faces west. Its five towers rise in a stepped pyramid meant to model Mount Meru, the mountain at the centre of the Hindu cosmos, ringed by galleries and a moat that stands for the encircling ocean. Millions of sandstone blocks were floated and hauled from quarries at Mount Kulen, some forty kilometres away; the binding technique between them is still not securely identified.

Work seems to have stopped around the king's death, leaving stretches of bas-relief unfinished — a hint of how tightly the project was bound to one reign. Angkor was sacked by Cham forces in 1177, and the capital was rebuilt to the north as Angkor Thom under Jayavarman VII, a Buddhist king. Angkor Wat drifted with the country into Theravada Buddhism over the following centuries and, alone among the great temples, was never wholly abandoned: monks remained, pilgrims came, and sixteenth-century Khmer inscriptions record restoration work. The wider city declined more slowly than the old story of sudden collapse allowed. Geoarchaeological evidence points to a thinning of land use through the fourteenth century rather than an abrupt emptying, and the Siamese capture of 1431 looks more like a punctuation mark than a cause. Why the hydraulic city faltered remains genuinely contested — decades-long droughts and floods recorded in tree rings, silting and neglect of the canals, the pull of trade toward the Mekong and the coast, and the religious shift away from temple-building kingship are all argued, and no single explanation commands agreement.

Portuguese travellers described the temple in the 1580s, and Chinese envoy Zhou Daguan had already left a vivid eyewitness account of Angkorian society in 1296, but it was the French naturalist Henri Mouhot's posthumously published notes of 1860 that fixed Angkor Wat in the European imagination — and with them the false but durable idea of a lost city reclaimed from the jungle. The École française d'Extrême-Orient began systematic clearance and conservation in 1908 and worked there, with interruptions, until the Cambodian civil war. The Khmer Rouge years left bullet damage and looted sculpture; a UNESCO World Heritage listing in 1992 brought back an international patchwork of restoration teams. Since 2012, airborne laser scanning has stripped away the tree canopy and revealed what stone monuments had hidden: house mounds, ponds, roads and field systems, including occupation inside the temple enclosure itself, which had long been assumed the preserve of priests.
significance: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument ever built, and it is the clearest surviving statement of a political idea that shaped mainland Southeast Asia for centuries — kingship as an earthly echo of divine order, made legible in stone, water and geometry. It also anchors a shift in how archaeologists think about pre-industrial cities: the low-density, water-managed settlement revealed around it has become a reference case for how large urban populations could be sustained without dense cores, and for how such systems become brittle under climate stress. For Cambodia, the temple has carried a heavier load still. It has appeared on the national flag under every regime since the nineteenth century, colonial, royalist, republican, Khmer Rouge and democratic alike, the one symbol none of them was willing to give up.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia articles on Angkor Wat and Angkor and general reference summaries; the dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped point in time. The deeper problem is the record itself: the Khmer left no narrative histories, and almost everything about Angkorian politics comes from Sanskrit and Old Khmer dedicatory inscriptions written to praise kings, supplemented by one foreign eyewitness account. Construction dates, the temple's original name, the size of its workforce, and the causes and pace of Angkor's decline are all reconstructed or contested rather than documented.
